newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Autoliv sees further price pressure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Autoliv sees further price pressure.

text.p: Newly merged Swedish/U.S. car safety equipment maker Autoliv Inc on Monday reported an improved first-half performance in line with market expectations but the company warned analysts that price pressure would continue to cap its style.

Analysts said sales were a little stronger than expected in the six months to June 30, rising three percent to $1.68 billion, while profit after financial items came roughly in line with expectations at $177 million against $161 million a year ago.

The only surprise in the report was a write-off for research and development acquired when Sweden's Autoliv AB merged with Morton International's car safety unit ASP which came in at $732.3 million against expectations of $555 million.
"This was somewhat higher than expected due to acquired research and development from Morton but no big deal," said analyst Mats Liss at Swedbank.
Autoliv's share price rose on the report but closed off its highs at 295.5 crowns, up 2.5 crowns. The share had risen to 302 on speculation ahead of the earnings report.
The company announced earnings per share rising to $1.01 from $0.90 and said it would pay a dividend of $0.11 per share on September 4.
The profit improvement stemmed largely from increased sales and continued productivity improvements, the company said.
"We are satisfied with the outcome of the first two months of the operations and for the first two quarters," chairman and chief executive Gunnar Bark told a telephone conference.
"You are never satisfied with all aspects of a company ... but so far I would not say we are disappointed in a significant way in any aspect of the combined company."
However Bark warned that price pressure was continuing in both Europe and most significantly in the U.S..
"We expect the price pressure (in the U.S.) to continue for half a year to one year," Bark said.
"We don't see (a fall of) two digit figures in Europe but it will be there in the U.S. for this year and early 1998."
Negative currency effects also took their toll in the first half of 1997.

While net profit rose 11 percent to $49 million for comparable units in the second quarter, Bark said underlying growth -- excluding the negative impact of the stronger dollar -- amounted to 15 percent.
"Key ratios are at good levels and even improving somewhat despite competition in the U.S. and negative currency effects from the strengthening U.S. dollar," he said.
Analyst Hans Westerberg from Den Danske Bank said the report gave the market no real disappointments or highlights.
He said the market was now waiting to see the costs of restructuring after the merger that will not be released until Autoliv releases its third quarter report on October 22.
"This will determine the share price in the future," he said.
"I think it is better that they do their homework first rather than adjust now."
-- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1017
